articles.title: Route app errors to the right Slack channel
articles.excerpt: The problem I kept hitting the same friction: rebuilding the same automation from scratch every time a slightly different event showed up. Copying a previous project helped for about an hour, and then…
articles.body: The problem I kept hitting the same friction: rebuilding the same automation from scratch every time a slightly different event showed up. Copying a previous project helped for about an hour, and then the small differences took over: different payload shapes, different failure modes, different places to look when nothing arrived. So I built 2026-10-28_error-alert-router to make the whole thing repeatable instead of memorable. How it works Webhook ( webhook ) — accepts the inbound event over HTTP and is the only entry point into the workflow. Keeping exactly one entry point is what makes the rest of the pipeline testable, because every execution starts from a request you can replay. Without it, events arrive through side doors and you end up debugging a shape you never designed for.

articles.body: If you work with LLM APIs you know the dance: you ask for working code, and you get a lecture. A disclaimer. Three paragraphs of "as an AI I cannot" followed by a suspiciously detailed explanation of why it cannot. I got tired of it, so I built armor-gw — a self-hosted, OpenAI-compatible proxy that sits between your app and any upstream model and refuses to accept refusals. How it works Every response passing through the gateway gets inspected by 13 detector classes.

articles.title: How we're testing AI app builders: database isolation, auth, usage and source export
articles.excerpt: I work on Uvilno. This is our evaluation protocol, not an independent leaderboard, and we have not completed a matched cross-product study. We publish the unknowns because a polished generated page is…
articles.body: I work on Uvilno. This is our evaluation protocol, not an independent leaderboard, and we have not completed a matched cross-product study. We publish the unknowns because a polished generated page is easy to confuse with a finished application. An AI builder can generate a plausible dashboard while its records disappear after reload. It can export a frontend while the identity service and database still live behind the vendor's API. It can say “fixed” while leaving the target button unchanged. Those are separate failure modes; a single aesthetic score obscures them. 1. Test persistence with two identities Use two app visitor accounts, A and B. As A, create a uniquely labelled private task, edit it and reload. Confirm the server returns the edited record.

To solve this for Amazon sellers, I built SellerScope Global — a free Chrome extension designed to streamline product research into a fast 3-step workflow. 🛠️ The Core Problem When evaluating an Amazon product, sellers need to quickly check: Sales Estimates & BSR: Is the product actually selling? articles.title: Local property prices in France, from recorded sales, in one command
articles.excerpt: Asking prices on listing sites show what sellers hope for. France also publishes what buyers actually paid: the DVF dataset (land value requests) on data.gouv.fr, free and without an API key. The catc…
articles.body: Asking prices on listing sites show what sellers hope for. France also publishes what buyers actually paid: the DVF dataset (land value requests) on data.gouv.fr, free and without an API key. The catch: raw files have one row per parcel and per dwelling, so a naive "price divided by surface" average counts some sales several times and mixes in garages, land and shops. I wrote a Hermes skill, area-market-analysis , that does the cleanup. It resolves a commune name to its INSEE code, downloads the yearly CSV files, groups rows by sale, and keeps only clean single-apartment or single-house sales for price statistics. Other sales (multi-unit, commercial, land) still count toward volume. Paris, Lyon and Marseille are expanded to arrondissements. Pure Python standard library.

articles.excerpt: A little light for the stories we never want to lose. What if AI could help us remember without pretending to be the people we miss? Memory Lantern is a memory garden built into the Dr. T platform. It…
articles.body: A little light for the stories we never want to lose. What I Built What if AI could help us remember without pretending to be the people we miss? Memory Lantern is a memory garden built into the Dr. T platform. It helps people preserve family stories, recipes, traditions, meaningful sayings, and moments of everyday joy, then weave selected memories into editable stories and tributes. For Hacktoberfest Week 4’s “Ghost in the Machine” theme, I chose a gentler interpretation of the ghost: not a digital imitation of someone who has passed away, but the traces people leave behind in their stories, voices, customs, and acts of love. Each memory becomes a lantern—a small light that can be revisited, organized, and shared intentionally.

articles.title: Kubernetes - Automated Dependency Updates with Renovate
articles.excerpt: This post is part of our ongoing series of posts for Kubernetes. In this post, we will automate dependency updates for our GitOps repository using Renovate, an open-source tool that finds outdated dep…
articles.body: This post is part of our ongoing series of posts for Kubernetes. In this post, we will automate dependency updates for our GitOps repository using Renovate , an open-source tool that finds outdated dependencies and raises pull requests to update them. All components in our cluster are pinned to a specific version: Helm charts in HelmRelease , Flux itself in gotk-components.yaml , and actions in our GitHub workflows. This is what GitOps expects, but nothing tells us when these versions become outdated. We hadn't touched our cluster for a while, and by the time we came back, every Helm chart had a newer release available. Checking release pages manually for each of them is error-prone and time-consuming.

articles.title: Google’s Genie 4 lets you build worlds that sound and move like real life
articles.excerpt: It's the first Google world model that can generate audio.
articles.body: TL;DR Google has announced the Genie 4 AI world model with realistic physics simulations. It is Google’s first real-time world model to support native audio generation. Genie 4 is currently in research preview and is only available to select trusted testers. It’s easy to think generative AI is all about video and image generation tools like Gemini Omni or Nano Banana. However, world models are where a lot of AI labs are focusing their research. World models build an internal simulation of the environment and use physics, spatial relationships, and time progression to create consistent output. While large language models (LLMs) use token data to predict the next word, world models predict how space, time, gravity, and other physical forces will evolve in an environment.

articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.

articles.excerpt: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s J…
articles.body: Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew members (from left) Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis, and James Spicer, pose for a photo on Oct. 8, 2025. Credit: NASA The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods to counter human spaceflight risks for future Artemis and Moon Base missions. Beginning at 3 p.m. EDT, NASA will provide live coverage of the volunteers’ departure from the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA, pronounced cha-pea’-ah) mission habitat.
